prose.detail:
On any of Frontend's five consignment party pickers, a search that matches nothing renders one line — "No addresses match your search." — and nothing else: no link, no button, no guidance (fe-address-picker-place-of-origin-no-matches). The only control left is "Save and continue", and submitting without a row selected returns "Select a consignor from the list" in an error summary (fe-address-picker-consignor-or-exporter-error), so the page cannot be satisfied at all. The picker form is a search input, a Search button, the results table, its pagination and Save and continue, and nothing more ([[c1]]); the addresses feature's copy holds no add-an-address key at all, the empty state's only string being noMatches ([[c2]]). The contact-address page is a different shape — the whole book as thirteen radios rather than a search — but it is the same dead end: it offers no way to add an address either (fe-contact). Searching the rendered DOM of every one of the 31 captured Frontend screens and 36 captured states for "add a new address", "add an address" or "address book" returns nothing. So a trader whose place of origin has never been saved cannot finish the addresses section, and the service gives them no way to find that out except by failing.

Design release 1 gives every address-selection page a route out to add one. On the five party pickers it is a secondary "Add a new address" button sitting under the results table and above "Save and continue" — six captured screens carry it, the five picker headings plus the search-filtered state — pointing at /address-book/add?from=<section> ([[c3]], with the href built at [[c4]]). On the contact-address page it is worded differently and sits above the radios, as a link inside the sentence "If the correct address is not shown, add a new branch address, then return to this page.", pointing at /address-book/add?from=contact-address. Following either skips the address-type chooser, because the section the user came from implies the type and is carried in a hidden addressType, and lands on "Add address details" (dr1-address-book-add-from-party-picker), where the address can be searched for or typed in by hand. Saving writes the address to the book, selects it into the section the user came from, redirects them back to that same page and shows a success message naming the address just added ([[c5]]). The notification is never abandoned.

Give every address-selection page a route out, and a return path back to it with the new address selected — the five pickers and the contact-address page. Nothing has to land first: the address-book API behind Frontend already serves create, and every other part of the picker exists. What a person has to choose is the destination, and it is the same choice this run's scope question turns on (address-book--saved-address-book-pages-absent) — either an add-address page inside this frontend, which means giving its address-book service a write path it deliberately does not have ([[c6]]), or a link out to the Import Notification Service front door's existing /address-book/add, which needs a return URL so the user comes back to the page they left rather than being stranded in another service's address book. The empty state's copy is part of the work either way: "No addresses match your search." is a statement with no next step in it.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding any link or button on a Frontend party picker or the contact-address page that leads to adding an address.

prose.detail:
On a Frontend party picker each row's "View details" is a disclosure that opens in place ([[c1]]), revealing the saved record as a plain list built from name, address lines, country, telephone number and email address ([[c2]]). The captured place-of-origin picker carries five of them, and the first opens to seven lines for Astra Rosales ending "01632 960000" and "astra-rosales@example.com". The row offers nothing else: no Edit, no Delete, no link out. So a trader who sees that a saved consignor has moved, that a postcode is wrong, or that the same farm is in the book twice, has no way to correct or remove it anywhere in this service, and the only thing they can do is pick the wrong record or abandon the section. Searching the rendered DOM of all 31 captured Frontend screens and 36 captured states for "edit address", "change this address", "edit this address" and "delete address" returns nothing. This is deliberate in the code: the address-book service exposes only search, all and party, and says "This service reads and never writes. The notification journey selects from the organisation's book; adding, changing and removing the records in it belongs to the INS frontend, which is the only writer" ([[c3]]). The transporter list is the same shape, its rows leading nowhere either.

In Design release 1 the same "View details" is a link out of the row to the saved address's own page, carrying the page the trader came from in a return parameter, so a row on the place-of-origin picker points at /address-book/<id>?return=%2Fplace-of-origin ([[c4]], with the href built at [[c5]]). That page is dr1-address-book-view: the record's name as the heading, a summary list of eight facts, and then an "Edit" button beside a red "Delete" button. Edit opens dr1-address-book-edit, headed "Edit address and contact details", with all nine address and contact fields prefilled and already open, the address search suppressed, and "Save changes" beside "Cancel"; the return parameter is carried into the form action, so saving or cancelling puts the trader back on the picker they left rather than stranding them in the address book, and the delete honours the same parameter. Design release 1's transporter list links its rows to the same record page. So in Design release 1 a wrong saved address is fixed where it is noticed, and the notification is never abandoned.

Give every picker row a route to the saved record and a way back to the page the trader left. This is the maintenance half of the route the add finding covers, and it turns on the same choice of destination: either an address record page inside this frontend, which means giving its address-book service the update and delete it deliberately does not have ([[c3]]), or a link into the Import Notification Service front door's existing address-book record and edit pages, which needs a return URL so the trader comes back to the picker. The address-book API already serves update and delete, so nothing has to land first either way and the band is frontend-work. Raise it separately from the add route because it is a different control, a different user need -- correcting or removing a record rather than creating one -- and because it was until now carried by nobody: the addresses slice recorded both "View details" behaviours and passed the question to address-book--saved-address-book-pages-absent, and the transport slice left Design release 1's transporter "View details" link out for the same reason, but neither that finding nor the add-route finding asks for the route. Whether the in-place disclosure survives alongside the link is a design call for whoever does the work; Design release 1 shows only the link. The named control, "View details", occurs five times on the Frontend picker and nine times on the Design release 1 one, so both cards will be refused a crop and fall back to the whole page with the reason printed. That is the right picture here: the finding is about what a row leads to, not about one row.

FALSIFIED BY: Finding any control on a Frontend party picker, transporter list or contact-address page that leads to changing or removing a saved address-book record.

prose.detail:
Frontend has no address book as a page. Its service navigation carries no items, so nothing links to a saved-addresses page, and searching the rendered DOM of all 31 captured Frontend screens and 36 captured states for "address book" or "add a new address" returns nothing. A trader meets the organisation's book only inside the five consignment party pickers and the contact-address page, and there only as a read-only chooser: the pickers offer a Search input hinted "Name, address or country", a secondary Search button, a five-row results table with a radio per row and a "View details" expander, pagination, and "Save and continue" ([[c1]]), and the contact-address page offers the whole book as one radio list. Nothing anywhere adds, changes or removes a record. Frontend's address-book service exposes only search, all and party, and states the split as a design decision: "This service reads and never writes. The notification journey selects from the organisation's book; adding, changing and removing the records in it belongs to the INS frontend, which is the only writer" ([[c2]]). Frontend's records also carry no address type at all, deliberately, because the same record may be a consignor on one notification and a consignee on the next ([[c3]]).

Design release 1 gives the trader an address book of their own, reached from a service-navigation item on every page, and eight captured screens describe it. dr1-address-book is the list: heading "Address book", intro "Manage your addresses for use across import notifications.", a primary "Add a new address" button, a "Filter addresses" panel holding a Search box placeholdered "Search by name, address or country" and a "Type" select offering Place of Origin, Consignor, Consignee, Importer, Place of Destination, Transporter and Branch Address, a result count ("Showing 1-8 of 58"), a Name / Type / Address / Country table with a "View" link per row, and pagination ([[c4]]). dr1-address-book-add is the type chooser: "What is the new address for?", one addressType radio group over those same seven types and a Continue button. Each type carries a hint that defines it, and the hints are as much of the requirement as the labels are, so they are quoted here in full — Place of Origin, "The address where the animals begin their journey to Great Britain"; Consignor, "This is the sender of the consignment."; Consignee, "This is the receiver or buyer of the consignment being shipped or transported."; Importer, "This is usually the same as the consignee. You can select a different person if needed."; Place of Destination, "This is where the animals will be unloaded and accommodated for at least 48 hours. If a health certificate is required, it will show this address."; Transporter, "This is the person or company responsible for transporting the consignment."; then a divider, and Branch Address, "This is the contact address of the person responsible for the consignment from when it enters Great Britain until authorities complete their checks." The labels, the hints and the divider are all defined together at [[c5]] and rendered as govuk-radios__hint at [[c6]]. dr1-address-book-lookup is the add form: "Add address details", a "Search for an address" type-ahead writing a hidden addressBookLookupAddressId, an "Enter address manually" toggle, "Save and continue" and "Cancel and return to address book". dr1-address-book-lookup-results is that page with the type-ahead panel open over candidate addresses. dr1-address-book-lookup-manual is that page with the manual reveal open, showing nine fields under two headings: Address (Name or organisation name, Address line 1, Address line 2 (optional), Town or city, County (optional), Postcode or Zip code, Country) and Contact details (Email address, Phone number, hinted "For international numbers include the country code"). dr1-address-book-add-from-party-picker is the same add form entered from a consignment party picker, with the type chooser skipped because the section implies the type and its answer carried in a hidden addressType. dr1-address-book-view is one saved address, headed with its own name, presented as a summary list of eight of those nine facts — County (optional) is not shown — with an "Edit" button and a red "Delete" button. dr1-address-book-edit is "Edit address and contact details": all nine fields, prefilled and already open, the search hidden, "Save changes" and "Cancel". So Design release 1's book is create, read, update and delete, and every saved address carries a type.

This is the one scope question in this comparison that a person has to settle, and it is stated here rather than decided. Two previous runs dropped these screens without photographing them; this run photographed all eight and they are enumerated above. The evidence for OUT of scope is strong, and it is not the reasoning either previous run used: the Import Notification Service front door, trade-imports-ins-frontend, already implements this address book at Design release 1's own URLs — /address-book, /address-book/add, /address-book/{id}, /address-book/{id}/edit and /address-book/{id}/delete — and its add form carries exactly the nine field labels above in Design release 1's wording, down to the phone hint; the address-book service behind it already serves create, update and delete; and this frontend's own service says writing belongs to that other service ([[c2]]). The evidence for IN scope is that Design release 1 puts the book behind a service-navigation item on the same service as the notification journey ([[c7]]) and routes into it from inside a notification ([[c8]]), so to a user it is one service and not two. What settles it is one thing a person can state: whether the trade-imports-ins-frontend address book is the address book Design release 1 describes. It is not yet the same book in one respect that the person deciding should know about: Design release 1 types every saved address and offers a Type filter over seven types, while the INS front door's add form asks for no type, its list has no Type column, and the address book API's locked wire contract (OperatorResponse in trade-imports-address-book) carries no type or role field — so whichever service owns these pages, the seven address types are unbuilt everywhere. If the INS book is Design release 1's book, this finding is struck and the work left in this repo is the route out of a party picker, raised separately as address-book--no-route-to-add-an-address-from-a-picker because it stands whichever way this goes, and the address types, raised separately as addresses--pickers-offer-the-whole-address-book because they bite inside the notification journey today. If it is not, this becomes one add-page piece of work covering all eight screens above, plus a write path in Frontend's address-book service. controls is deliberately empty: the finding is that eight whole pages have no counterpart, and cropping any single control on them would show less than the page does.

prose.detail:
Every unanswered row on the Consignment addresses page offers one action, "Add", which opens that party's picker. There is no way to reuse an address already chosen for another party: the row's action list holds a single link built from the party's slug ([[c1]]), and no captured frontend screen or state contains the string "Same as". The page even carries the hint that invites the shortcut — the Importer row reads "This is usually the same as the consignee. You can select a different person if needed." — and then offers no way to say "the same". A trader whose importer, consignee and place of destination are one company searches the book and picks the same row three times.

Design release 1 puts a second action beside "Add" on exactly the rows where a copy makes sense, and only once there is something to copy. When a consignee has been chosen, the Importer and Place of destination rows each gain a "Same as consignee" control; when a place of origin has been chosen, the Consignor row gains "Same as place of origin" ([[c2]], availability decided at [[c3]]). Pressing it fills that row in place, from the same page, with no picker in between; the row then shows the copied address and a "Change" link like any other.

Add a copy-from-another-party action to the Consignment addresses page: "Same as place of origin" on the Consignor row, "Same as consignee" on the Importer and Place of destination rows, each shown only when the source party has been answered and the target has not. prose.detail:
All five party pickers and the contact-address page draw from one undifferentiated list. Every captured picker reports "Showing 5 of 13 addresses" and every one of them offers the same thirteen records in the same order, whether the trader is choosing a place of origin abroad or a consignee in Great Britain — the place-of-origin picker and the consignee picker both lead with Astra Rosales in Switzerland, Tech Imports Ltd in London and Origin Farm in Ireland. Those two pickers are byte-identical in the captured DOM — same caption, same five rows in the same order, the remaining eight behind the same pagination — so the page that asks for the farm the animals left offers Great Britain importers, and the page that asks who is receiving them offers foreign farms. The contact-address page lists the same book again, all thirteen as radios ([[c1]], which calls `addressBook.all`). This is deliberate: the address-book service states that addresses have no type, because the same record may be a consignor on one notification and a consignee on the next, and so no function it exposes takes a role ([[c2]]). The picker controller calls the book with a query and a page number and nothing else ([[c3]]), so no amount of real data changes what these pages offer: there is no field to filter on. The consequence for the trader is that every picker asks them to find the right kind of address in a list that is mostly the wrong kind, with nothing on the page marking which is which.

Design release 1 types every saved address and filters each picker to its type. Place of origin offers nine foreign farms, consignor nine, consignee six Great Britain importers, importer six, place of destination three — different lists, from the same book, with the section's own type deciding what appears ([[c4]] and [[c5]]). The types are the trader's own: saving an address begins by asking "What is the new address for?" over Place of Origin, Consignor, Consignee, Importer, Place of Destination, Transporter and, after a divider, Branch Address ([[c6]]). The contact address is the Branch Address type, held as its own list of the organisation's branches ([[c7]]), which is why Design release 1's contact page says "add a new branch address" rather than "add an address".

Give a saved address one or more roles and filter each picker by the role it is asking for, including the contact page, which asks only for a branch address. The frontend cannot do this alone: its address-book service reads a book that carries no type at all and exposes no role-aware call ([[c8]]), so the address-book API — the Standard Address Block records in trade-imports-address-book — has to carry the type first, and whichever service writes those records has to collect it. Decide it together with the address-book scope question raised as address-book--saved-address-book-pages-absent, because the type is collected on the add form that question is about. This is a live defect in the notification journey whichever way that scope question is settled: it is about what the pickers Frontend already has show today, not about pages Frontend does not have, so it survives a ruling that the eight address-book screens belong to another service. Until the type exists, no useful half of this can ship: filtering on a guess, such as matching the country against the direction of travel, would hide addresses the trader legitimately wants. `controls` is deliberately empty: what differs is which rows are in the table, so the whole table on each of two pickers is the shot, and the only named control on those rows, `party`, occurs once per row and would be refused a crop.

prose.detail:
One identifier is enough. A trader who fills the ear tag and leaves the passport blank presses "Save and add another", the animal is added to the summary list as "Animal 1 — Ear tag: UK123456789012", and the counter moves on. Only an entirely empty animal is refused, with "Enter at least one identifier for this animal" ([[c1]]), which is the rule the obligation states as a requires-any-of over the six identifier fields ([[c2]]). fe-animal-identification-saved and fe-animal-identification-at-maximum both show animals saved on an ear tag alone.

Design release 1 appears to require all of them. An animal counts as entered only when every identifier declared for its commodity carries a value ([[c3]]), so a cattle animal needs both an ear tag and a passport. A partly filled animal is not refused and no error is shown — the page simply re-renders the same animal with the values kept and the counter unmoved, and the saved-animals table lists only complete animals. That is a silent outcome rather than a stated rule, which is what makes this finding uncertain.

This is disputed because the two sources of the requirement disagree, and the two readings imply opposite work: if all identifiers are required, Frontend has to change its requires-any-of to a requires-all per commodity and write the error copy for it; if they are not, Frontend is already right and this finding should be struck. Design release 1's behaviour is not in doubt — its entry form holds a trader on an animal until every identifier for that commodity carries a value, and its saved list only ever shows complete animals. What is in doubt is whether that behaviour states a requirement, because the data-fields specification Frontend implements says the opposite in words: the obligation carries the V4 line "Field Block - Mandatory to Submit - At least one Animal Identifier" ([[c4]]). The one observation that would settle it is a statement from the design authority on which of the two governs — Design release 1's silent per-field behaviour, or the V4 field block. No capture can settle it; see the correction for why the capture originally proposed here cannot fire.

prose.detail:
The port-of-exit select is the port-of-entry list. Its captured DOM offers about eighty entries running from "Aberdeen Airport (GB DYC)" to the far end of the alphabet, including inland and cargo terminals such as "Nottingham Port (GB NTG)" and "HES Humber Bulk Terminal (GB HMR)", and the page says so out loud: the field's hint reads "Choose where the consignment will leave Great Britain. The controller builds the options by mapping the single shared ports service ([[c2]]) and validates the answer against that same list ([[c3]]); the service holds one list and primes it from the reference-data service's ports-of-entry endpoint ([[c4]]). There is no exit list and no filter over the entry list. The frontend's own obligation records where the decision came from: "Port selected from the port of entry list (Exit and Entry share the same list)" at [[c5]].

The port of exit is a short, purpose-built list of ten border control posts approved to handle animals: Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, three Heathrow posts, Holyhead, Manchester, Prestwick and Stansted, each carrying its BCP code. Design release 1 keeps it in its own file, separate from the arrival ports, and names it for what it is ([[c6]]). It is following a different requirements source, the V4 field spec quoted in its own obligation, which says exit and entry share a list. prose.detail:
A trader cannot submit until every animal on every commodity line has an identifier record. The animal-identifier group carries a count rule as well as a content rule: each unit record must hold at least one of the six identifiers, and the number of unit records on a commodity line must equal the number of animals declared for that line ([[c1]], `recordCountEquals` against `numberOfAnimals`). That group is the whole of the `animalIdentification` task row ([[c2]]), and readiness demands every task row be fulfilled, not applicable or optional ([[c3]]). Readiness is the gate on both the review section ([[c4]]) and the submit itself, which returns `ok: false` and goes nowhere without it ([[c5]]). So a trader who declares twenty animals must fill in twenty identifier cards before the service will take the notification. Documents are the one thing Frontend does let through: the documents group carries no minimum, so an empty collection is not a bar.

Design release 1 asks for none of it. Its submit gate ends with the line "Documents remain optional. Animal identifiers are optional unless multiple species are selected, in which case at least one identifier is required per species" ([[c6]]). The minimum returns true outright for a single-species consignment however many identifier fields that commodity carries, and for a multi-species one it asks for a single complete entry per species, never one per animal ([[c7]]). The captured review page is the proof: a notification of five Bison bison with no identifier saved shows an empty "Bison Bison" card under "Identification details", no error summary, and a live Continue button. Design release 1 then chases what is missing rather than refusing it — the submitted page carries "You still need to:" with "complete the animal identifier information in the notification" as a bullet.

Move the animal-identifier requirement out of the submit gate and into the follow-up. The shared layout renders breadcrumbs and then a Back link, one under the other ([[c1]]). 57 of the 67 captured frontend screens show both. On the origin page the trail reads "Your notifications" then "Origin of the import", and a "Back" link sits directly beneath it. The confirmation page shows the trail with no Back link. The trail is always two levels and never names the notification it belongs to ([[c2]]). The overview is the only journey page that opts out, by passing breadcrumbs: false. Design release 1 gives every card the same two links whatever its status, side by side after the reference and separated by a divider: "Copy as new" and "View" ([[c2]], which carries no status condition of any kind). There is no unsorted state anywhere in the dashboard. Every option in the select names an ordering, and one of them is always in force: the controller parses the sort query parameter and falls back to a default when it is absent or unrecognised ([[c1]], through parseNotificationSort at [[c2]]), and the picture of fe-dashboard-populated shows "Arrival (newest to oldest)" already selected on a page the trader has not touched. The default is carried all the way to the notification list read, which defaults the parameter again and interpolates it unconditionally into the request ([[c3]] and [[c4]]). So a trader cannot see the list in the order the service returns it, and the page never has to answer the question of what to show when nothing has been chosen.

Design release 1's select loads on "Select one", an unselected placeholder ahead of its three orderings ([[c5]]), and the captured DOM of dr1-dashboard shows it selected. So the design's starting state is a list with no ordering named. The design does not say what that order should be, and it cannot be read off the prototype: getDashboardViewModel reads the sort parameter, hands it to buildDashboardSortItems so the right option shows as selected and to the pagination hrefs, and never orders the notification list by it ([[c6]]), so the prototype's list is in fixture order whatever the select says.

Give the dashboard a state in which no ordering has been chosen, and decide what the list query does in it. Two things have to happen in Frontend. The sort control needs an unselected entry that is not an ordering, which means the default at [[c7]] stops being applied when the trader has chosen nothing rather than being applied silently. Then the notification list read has to be able to ask for a page without an ordering: [[c3]] defaults sort to arrivalDate,desc and [[c4]] puts it in the query string on every call, so the parameter has to become optional there and the stub at [[c8]] has to match. The band is frontend-work because both edits are Frontend's and the frontend can build and run this against its own stub today — but confirm with the notifications API's owners what order it returns when no sort parameter is sent before this ships, because that order is what a trader will actually see and neither this design nor the prototype specifies it. Adding the "Select one" label to the options list is part of the copy change raised as service-wide--dashboard-sort-orderings-differ; this finding is what the label has to mean.

Almost every journey page ends with a primary button reading "Save and continue", which is what the shared button macro renders when a page passes no primary of its own ([[c1]], reading [[c2]]). Four pages pass their own primary and label it just "Continue", and between them they account for twelve of the sixty-seven captured frontend screens: the accompanying-documents page in all four of its captured states (fe-documents, fe-documents-populated, fe-documents-scanning, fe-documents-error), the consignment addresses hub in all three (fe-addresses-hub, fe-addresses-hub-empty, fe-addresses-hub-complete), check your answers in all three (fe-check-answers, fe-check-answers-incomplete, fe-check-answers-submitted) and the declaration in both (fe-declaration, fe-declaration-error). The two overrides that matter are [[c3]] and [[c4]], each reading a per-feature copy key set to the string "Continue" at [[c5]] and [[c6]]. On both of those pages the "Continue" button sits immediately to the left of a secondary button reading "Save and return to hub", so the page offers the user a choice between a button that says it saves and a button that does not.

Design release 1 ends the same two pages with "Save and continue". Upload documents states it at [[c7]] and the consignment addresses hub at [[c8]], and both render it beside a secondary "Save and return to overview". Design release 1 does use a bare "Continue" — but only on two pages, and they are the two at the end of the journey where there is nothing left to save: review your notification ([[c9]]) and the declaration ([[c10]]), each of which ends with that single button and no secondary. Change the two per-feature copy keys from "Continue" to "Save and continue": [[c5]] and [[c6]]. The documents override must stay in place because it also carries name="action" and value="continue", which the post dispatcher branches on; only its text changes. The addresses override carries nothing else, so that page can drop its primary argument at [[c4]] and fall through to the macro's default instead. Seven captured screens change: the four documents states and the three addresses hub states. FIVE MUST NOT CHANGE. Check your answers and the declaration already read "Continue" on both sides, because Design release 1 reads "Continue" there too — so fe-check-answers, fe-check-answers-incomplete, fe-check-answers-submitted, fe-declaration and fe-declaration-error are already right and renaming them would introduce a difference that does not exist today. This is not a service-wide rename; it is two copy keys. Two boundaries with neighbouring findings, because a corpus-wide duplicate sweep has already run and this is a new near-neighbour. First: service-wide--save-and-cancel-buttons-name-the-hub renames the two controls to the RIGHT of this button — "Save and return to hub" and "Cancel and return to hub" — which come from the shared keys at [[c11]] and change on every page at once. This finding is the button to their left, which comes from each page's own copy and changes on two pages. Different strings, different files, different blast radius. Second: documents--continue-discards-a-filled-in-document says that pressing this button on the documents page throws away a document the trader has filled in but not added. These two must land together or the copy one must land second, because renaming the button to "Save and continue" while it still discards makes the label state something untrue. One further difference runs the other way and is already recorded elsewhere: on two pages Design release 1 reads "Continue" where the frontend reads "Save and continue" — the contact address page and the transporter-type page — and that is inside service-wide--save-and-cancel-shown-where-the-design-shows-one-button, whose own screens are those pages and whose change removes the surrounding controls at the same time. It is deliberately not folded in here.

prose.detail:
The question is compulsory once it applies. `transitedCountries` is in scope and mandatory whenever the means of transport is rail or a road vehicle ([[c1]]), so a trader who presses Save and continue without ticking a box gets the page back with "There is a problem" and the message "Select at least one country the consignment will travel through", both in the error summary and above the checkbox list ([[c2]]). The notification cannot be submitted until a country is chosen, because the transit-countries task row has to be fulfilled like every other in-scope row.

Design release 1 asks the same question of the same traders and accepts no answer to it. Its transit-countries handler runs no validation of any kind: it clears any errors, saves whatever was posted — including an empty list — and moves on ([[c3]]). Its completeness check for the section is a function that returns a literal true with the comment "Transit countries are optional — any saved list (including empty) is acceptable" ([[c4]]), and the section is absent from the ten predicates that gate submission. So a road or rail consignment reaches the declaration with no transit country recorded, and nothing anywhere tells the trader one was expected.

Make the transit-countries answer optional. In [[c1]] the in-scope branch keeps `inScope: true` and its reason but drops `status: 'mandatory'`, so the question is still asked of rail and road consignments and still purged for the others, but an empty selection no longer holds the task row out of fulfilled and no longer blocks submission. The "Select at least one country the consignment will travel through" message then has nothing to fire on and goes with it, along with the error state of the page. Nothing has to land first — the obligation and its copy are both frontend files, and the notification contract already carries an empty list. Note that this is a change to whether the question must be answered, not to how it is asked: replacing the checkbox list with a search-and-add control is transport--transit-countries-is-a-checkbox-list, and that work should carry this rule rather than the current one.

The transporter authorisation guidance opens the transporter type page: the lead sentence about DAERA and APHA, three bullets, a guidance link, and two closing sentences. The link reads "Find out how to transport animals in connection with an economic activity (opens in new tab)" and goes to https://www.gov.uk/guidance/transporting-animals-in-great-britain, which is the general page on transporting animals in Great Britain. The last sentence reads "Documents issued in any EU Member State are not valid for use in GB." The whole block is one copy object at [[c1]], rendered at [[c2]].

Design release 1 shows the same guidance, in the same order, at the top of its transporter page ([[c3]]). The lead sentence and all three bullets match the frontend word for word. Two lines do not. The link reads "…(opens in a new tab)" and goes to the animal-welfare-in-transport guidance, anchored at its section on transporting animals in connection with an economic activity — a different page, and one that lands the user on the specific section rather than at the top of a general one. The last sentence reads "Documents issued in any EU member state are not valid for use in GB.", in sentence case.

Bring the transporter authorisation guidance block into line with Design release 1: point the guidance link at https://www.gov.uk/guidance/animal-welfare-in-transport#transporting-animals-in-connection-with-an-economic-activity, change its text to end "(opens in a new tab)", and lower-case "member state" in the closing sentence. All three strings sit in the one guidance object at [[c1]], so this is a single edit to a single block rather than three scattered ones. Take the href from Design release 1 without the Google Analytics linker parameters its prototype copy carries — those are an artefact of how the URL was pasted, not part of the requirement. Where the block ends up on the page is settled by the flow change raised beside this one, which moves the guidance onto the transporter list; this finding is only about what it says.

prose.detail:
The transporter section opens on a page that begins with the DAERA and APHA authorisation guidance and only then asks the question. Below that guidance sits the heading "What type of transporter will move the animals?", hinted "We will ask for the transporter's details next.", with two radios, Commercial ("A business approved to transport animals — you will choose one from a list") and Private ("You or another individual moving the animals — you will give their address"). The answer forks the journey: Commercial goes to a list of approved commercial transporters to pick one from, Private goes to a blank name-and-address form. The two branches never meet, so a user whose transporter is already known to the service but is a private one has no list to pick it from and types the whole address again. The order and the fork are declared as three consecutive pages in one section at [[c1]], and the copy at [[c2]].

The transporter section opens on one page headed "Transporter details", introduced "This is the person or company responsible for transporting the consignment.", carrying the same DAERA and APHA guidance apart from the wording and destination of its guidance link, then "Select a transporter" over a searchable table of every transporter the trader can use. The table mixes both kinds: Yusen Logistics (Romania) SRL, Roadtrain Ltd, Danish Meat Export ApS and Portuguese Livestock Lda are typed Commercial, and Aberdeen Livestock Ltd, Romanian Agri Exports SRL, Slovak Farm Export and Finnish Livestock Oy are typed Private. A user picks a row and continues. Only a user who cannot find their transporter presses "Add a transporter", and only then is the type question asked, on a separate page headed "Choose a transporter type" warned "Before you add this transporter, please ensure you have already searched for it first." ([[c3]]). The linear journey holds one transporter step, /transporter ([[c4]]); both add pages sit off it.

Restructure the transporter section so the list comes first and the type question comes second. The frontend needs one transporter page that lists every transporter available to the trader, commercial and private, with the DAERA and APHA guidance and the "This is the person or company responsible for transporting the consignment" introduction on it, and a route off that page for adding one that is not listed. The type chooser then moves off the linear journey onto that add route, asked only of a trader who could not find their transporter in the list, and the two branches it forks into become the two ways of adding a transporter rather than the two ways of choosing one. The words on the chooser and on the private form it leads to also change, and that is raised separately as transport--transporter-type-chooser-copy-differs so it can land on the pages as they stand today without waiting for this. This is the parent of four other transport findings and should land before them: the list needs a search box, the list needs Type and Status per row, the add route needs a commercial form, and the chooser needs Design release 1's copy. Nothing outside the frontend has to change first — the list is a local fixture at [[c5]] and it can be widened to carry private transporters there.

It offers two radios in this order: Commercial, hinted "A business approved to transport animals — you will choose one from a list", then Private, hinted "You or another individual moving the animals — you will give their address". The copy is at [[c1]] and the captured DOM of fe-transporter-type carries all of it verbatim. The page a trader reaches by answering Private is headed "Private transporter details" ([[c2]]), again with no caption.

Design release 1 heads the same question "Choose a transporter type" under a caption reading "Add a new transporter", and puts a warning between the heading and the radios: "Before you add this transporter, please ensure you have already searched for it first." ([[c3]]). The fieldset legend is visually hidden, so the heading does the work. The radios are the other way round — Private transporter first with no hint at all, then Commercial with one hint, "This can only be a commercial transporter from Northern Ireland." — and the labels differ too: "Private transporter" rather than "Private". The page reached by answering Private is headed "Add private transporter" under the same "Add a new transporter" caption ([[c4]]).

Rewrite the type question's copy to match Design release 1 and rename the private form's heading with it. On the type page: change the heading to "Choose a transporter type", add the caption "Add a new transporter" above it, add a warning reading "Before you add this transporter, please ensure you have already searched for it first.", drop the "We will ask for the transporter's details next." hint, reverse the two options so Private transporter comes first, relabel Private as "Private transporter", drop both of the frontend's explanatory hints and give Commercial the single hint "This can only be a commercial transporter from Northern Ireland." All of that is [[c1]] and the template that reads it. On the private form: change the heading at [[c2]] from "Private transporter details" to "Add private transporter" and add the same "Add a new transporter" caption. This is copy on two pages Frontend already has and the band is frontend-work. It is independently schedulable from transport--transporter-type-asked-before-any-list, which moves the type question off the linear journey and onto an add route: the copy can be corrected on the page where it stands today, and the flow can be restructured without any of the copy changing. Note one thing for whoever schedules them together — Design release 1's warning tells the trader to search first, which only makes sense once the searchable list that flow change introduces exists, so if the copy lands alone the warning is the one sentence that will read oddly until it does.
